Lawsuits pour in as new California law opens window for bringing old child sex abuse claims

With courthouses open for business Thursday, Craig Griffin joined other middle-aged Californians lining up to file

lawsuits over sexual assault they say they suffered as children. A state law that took effect New Year’s Day opens

a “window” for such claims that otherwise would be too old to bring in court.

“I can remember that really well, but I never told anybody,” Griffin said in an interview last month as he prepared his

case, filed Thursday in Contra Costa County Superior Court. “I felt ashamed.”

Boy Scouts of America, headquartered in Irving, Texas, said in response Thursday that “we care deeply about all

victims of child abuse and sincerely apologize to anyone who was harmed during their time in Scouting.”

“We are outraged that there have been times when individuals took advantage of our programs to abuse innocent 

children,” Boy Scouts of America said. ”We believe victims, we support them, we pay for unlimited counseling by a

provider of their choice, and we encourage them to come forward. It is BSA policy that all incidents of suspected

abuse are reported to law enforcement.”

The Scouting organization, which has more than 2.1 million youth members ages 7 to 21 and nearly 1 million adult

volunteers in local councils throughout the United States and its territories, would not comment specifically on Griffin’s allegations.

The state law, AB 218, allows victims of alleged childhood sexual assault to file lawsuits over the next three years that

otherwise would be barred by the statute of limitations. It also greatly extends the time adults who realize they were

molested as kids have to file a claim, from age 26 to 40, or five years instead of three from the time they realize

the abuse harmed them psychologically.

Law firms specializing in such cases have been preparing to begin filing this year. Lawyers representing Griffin

filed five cases Thursday and said they anticipate some 4,000 cases against institutions including the Boy Scouts

and Roman Catholic church.

Attorney Jeff Anderson earlier this week announced lawsuits on behalf of two people who claim they were molested

by two priests in the Diocese of Oakland. His firm also announced suits on behalf of a man who said he was abused

at age 13 in the 1970s by a priest at Bellarmine College Preparatory School in San Jose, and another alleging abuse by

a Palma High School priest in Salinas in the 1980s. His firm has filed a dozen suits so far, including one Thursday involving

a Catholic school in Bakersfield, and is planning legal action against other California dioceses and one religious order in

the coming weeks.

“This is just kind of the first wave,” said Mike Reck, a lawyer with the Anderson firm.

Opponents of the law, including school organizations, their attorneys and insurers, argued it was a gift to plaintiff

lawyers that will subject schools and other organizations to costly, older claims they cannot defend against because

those records and witnesses are unavailable or unreliable. Former Gov. Jerry Brown had vetoed similar bills. The law by Assemblywoman Lorena Gonzalez, D-San Diego, was supported by police chiefs and victim advocates.

Griffin’s case illustrates what the law’s backers argued is a common predicament for abused children who often are

unable for decades to understand the impact the abuse had on them.

Griffin said the alleged abuse occurred in the mid-1970s when he was about 9 or 10 and had joined a Cub Scout group

in Pinole, where he attended elementary school. He remembers the troop number and even some of the kids’ names.

Griffin said one scout’s parents who served as “den” leaders had them play games at their home, such as hide-and-seek.

On at least two occasions during those games, he said, there was sexual touching over their clothes or underwear. Both

parents, he said, were involved in abusing the boys.

“We were all touching each other — it was weird, but as a kid I didn’t think nothing of it,” Griffin said. He only told his

mother at the time, who promptly yanked him out of the program. He said he also had been molested by a relative

and was unable to discuss it with anyone else until 2010, when he confided in a sister. “I never knew who to talk to

about that,” Griffin said. “I didn’t want to think about it any more.” Griffin’s lawsuit identifies the accused organizations

and individuals only as nameless “Does,” which Jason P. Amala, one of his lawyers, said is due to a requirement in

the law that allows a judge to review the credibility of the claims first.

But the complaint makes clear the allegations involve Boy Scouts of America.

The complaint alleges the adults who served as Cub Scout leaders or volunteers for Boy Scouts of America used

their positions “to groom and to sexually abuse Plaintiff Craig Griffin” multiple times, and that the organization knew

or should have known of such dangers. It seeks unspecified damages for sexual abuse, negligence and emotional distress.

Griffin, who said he’s a recovering addict, believes the abuse he suffered as a child derailed his life.
